articles.author: Rausal Bahtiar Fadhli
articles.description:
Breach Notification Pipeline Against a Fixed Regulatory Deadline


Breach notification is a race against a statutory clock, not a writing task. Singapore PDPA guidance and GDPR Article 33 converge on the same constraint: assessment and regulator notification inside a fixed window. Automation wins that race only when the pipeline is built before the incident, because the clock starts at discovery, not at the first meeting.
A notification pipeline that depends on human kickoff loses the first hours to coordination. Triage calls, spreadsheet trackers, and legal review queues consume the window that regulators measure. The pipeline must start from a machine event: a detection alert that opens a timestamped case record with the deadline computed and written into the case row itself.

You exported OHLCV from a free source, pointed your backtest at it, and got an equity curve. The problem: free and exported data ships with duplicate timestamps, gaps, mixed timezones and adjustment artifacts — and backtesting engines don't complain, they just eat it. Here's the cleaning pass I'd run on any OHLCV file before trusting a single trade signal from it.

Short answer: to split a video with FFmpeg, use the segment muxer:
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -map 0 -c copy -f segment -segment_times 4.041667,7.083333 -reset_timestamps 1 part_%03d.mp4

That is lossless and fast, but with -c copy FFmpeg can only cut on keyframes, so -segment_time 2 does not mean "2-second parts". If you need exact lengths you must re-encode and force a keyframe at every boundary. Below are the measurements on a real 10-second clip, a small Python module, and five pytest checks that prove the parts add back up to the source.

The Microsoft 365 outage of 12–14 November 2026 was an engineering failure, not an attack. Microsoft says so, and I have no evidence to the contrary.
Microsoft listed Defender XDR among the affected services. The same dependency that carried email also carried part of the security tooling watching it.
Whether detections were actually lost is not public yet. That uncertainty is the blind spot.
You can't fix this by trusting a vendor harder. You fix it with an out-of-band logging path, a degraded-mode runbook, and a habit of treating "no alerts" as a claim to verify.

articles.author: FinnianFox8297
articles.description:
Short answer: for a Node.js SaaS that sends a weekly digest to active logistics customers, start with a durable queue, an explicit rate limiter, idempotent delivery records, and bounded exponential backoff; choose the cheapest simple option only after it can prove those delivery guarantees.
I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. The failure pattern is predictable: a timer fires, a webhook is sent, the process dies before recording the result, and the next retry sends the same business event again. The opposite failure is just as bad. A retry loop ignores the receiver's rate limit, turns a small outage into a queue storm, and delays every customer's digest.
The useful unit of design is not “a cron job.” It is a delivery attempt with a durable identity, a deadline, and a …
